# Cold engine works on three out of four cylinders

This behavior is a classic diagnostic signature in internal combustion engines, specifically pointing toward an intake air leak or a fuel delivery issue that only manifests when thermal expansion is minimal. The fact that the engine runs smoothly once warm indicates the core componentsâspark plugs, ignition coils, and the crankcaseâare mechanically sound. The problem lies in the system's response to cold temperatures, where clearances tighten and fluid viscosity increases.

The most probable culprit is a vacuum leak at the intake manifold gasket or a cracked PCV hose. When the engine is cold, the metal of the intake manifold contracts slightly due to lower ambient temperatures. If there is even a microscopic gap in the gasket seal, this contraction creates a path for unmetered air to enter the engine. This extra air bypasses the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor or the Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) sensor, causing the Engine Control Unit (ECU) to calculate a fuel mixture that is too lean based on the oxygen sensor feedback.

As the engine warms up, the metal expands back into its designed clearance gap, sealing the leak naturally. The ECU then returns to managing a stoichiometric ratio across all cylinders, and the misfire disappears. This thermal dependency rules out mechanical failures like stuck valves or broken pistons, which would persist regardless of temperature.

To diagnose this systematically, you should inspect all vacuum lines for cracks, brittleness, or loose connections. Pay special attention to the Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) valve and hose, as these are common failure points on older Honda engines. You can also perform a smoke test while the engine is cold; if smoke is drawn into the intake manifold through a specific port, you have located the leak source.

Another potential cause involves the throttle body gasket or the idle air control valve (IAC) seat. On some models, carbon buildup around the IAC valve can prevent it from fully sealing when the actuator is in its closed position during cold start modes. If the seal isn't perfect, air rushes in, leaning out the mixture for the affected cylinder group. Cleaning the throttle body and ensuring the gasket seats correctly often resolves this without replacing parts.

Fuel system issues are less likely but possible. A failing fuel injector might not spray adequately when the fuel is cold and viscous, though usually, this affects all cylinders or causes a rough idle rather than a specific three-cylinder operation. However, if one injector is clogged with varnish that hasn't been dissolved by a warm-up cycle, it could theoretically act similarly to a vacuum leak until the fuel thins out.

If you are comfortable with electronics, checking for Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) using an OBD-II scanner while the engine is cold is a smart first step. Look for codes related to lean conditions (e.g., P0171, P0172) or cylinder misfires (P030X series). These codes can tell you if the ECU has already detected the imbalance before you even notice the rough idle.

Ultimately, the solution involves addressing the physical gaps that open up when the engine cools. Replacing aged rubber hoses with silicone equivalents is often a cost-effective fix, as they retain elasticity better in cold weather and resist cracking over time. If the issue persists after replacing vacuum lines and cleaning the throttle body, inspecting the intake manifold gasket for replacement becomes the next logical step.
